title: Automatic Differentiation
description: How software computes exact derivatives of programs: computational graphs, forward mode with dual numbers, reverse mode, a small implementation and the practice of PyTorch and JAX.
overview: Training a model by gradient descent needs the gradient of the loss with respect to every parameter. For a neural network the loss is a long composition of simple operations, and deriving its gradient by hand for each new architecture would be tedious and error-prone. Automatic differentiation (AD) computes the derivative of a program mechanically, exactly (to rounding error) and at a cost comparable to running the program itself. It is the engine of every deep learning framework.

This chapter explains the idea from the chain rule, derives the two modes (forward and reverse), builds a working reverse-mode engine in about thirty lines of Python, and describes how the major frameworks use it. It is the computational counterpart of the Backpropagation chapter of the Machine Learning book, which derives the same computation for a fully connected network.
objectives: Compare symbolic, numerical and automatic differentiation by accuracy and cost.
Evaluate a function and its derivative by hand along a computational graph in forward mode and in reverse mode.
Explain why reverse mode is efficient for scalar losses with many parameters, and state the memory cost.
Implement forward mode with dual numbers and a small reverse-mode engine.
Use autograd in PyTorch or JAX, and avoid the common pitfalls.

sections.title: Three ways to differentiate a program
body: Suppose you have a program that computes a loss from a thousand parameters, and you need to know how the loss changes when each parameter is nudged. You could nudge each one and rerun the program (slow), derive formulas by hand (error-prone), or have the computer apply the rules of calculus mechanically to the very steps of the program. The last is automatic differentiation, and it is what makes training large models practical. To get the derivative of a function written as a program there are three approaches.

body: Finite differences are easy but inaccurate and expensive: a model with 10⁶ parameters would need a million forward passes for one gradient (see Numerical Computing for the choice of h). Symbolic differentiation returns a formula, which is not what a program with loops, branches and data-dependent control flow supplies. **Automatic differentiation** works on the program itself. Every program, however complicated, executes a sequence of elementary operations (addition, multiplication, exp, log, sin) whose derivatives are known. AD applies the chain rule to that sequence.

body.note: AD is not symbolic: it never builds a formula for the derivative. It computes the numerical value of the derivative at the given input, alongside the value of the function.

check.q: Compared with finite differences, automatic differentiation is
check.a: exact up to rounding and much cheaper for many inputs
wrong: exact but requires a symbolic formula

sections.title: The computational graph and the evaluation trace
body: Break the function into elementary steps, each producing an intermediate variable v_i from earlier ones. This sequence is the **evaluation trace** (or Wengert list), and the dependence between variables is the **computational graph** (see Computational graphs in the Backpropagation chapter).

example.title: An evaluation trace
example.problem: Write f(x₁, x₂) = ln(x₁) + x₁x₂ − sin(x₂) as a trace and evaluate it at (x₁, x₂) = (2, 5).
solution: So f(2, 5) = 11.652. By hand the derivatives are ∂f/∂x₁ = 1/x₁ + x₂ = 0.5 + 5 = 5.5 and ∂f/∂x₂ = x₁ − cos x₂ = 2 − 0.2837 = 1.7163. AD finds the same numbers mechanically, in two ways.

body: Each elementary operation has a known local derivative: for v = a + b, ∂v/∂a = ∂v/∂b = 1; for v = a·b, ∂v/∂a = b and ∂v/∂b = a; for v = ln a, ∂v/∂a = 1/a; for v = sin a, ∂v/∂a = cos a. The two modes differ in the direction in which the chain rule is accumulated through the trace.

check.q: Why can AD handle programs with loops and branches?
check.a: It differentiates the sequence of elementary operations that actually executed
wrong: It requires the program to be a single formula

sections.title: Forward mode and dual numbers
body: Forward mode answers the question: if I nudge one input, how does every later quantity respond? Imagine pushing on one domino and watching the effect travel down the line. Each value carries along a second number, how fast it is changing, and every operation updates both together. The cost is one pass per input you nudge, which is cheap when there are few inputs and expensive when there are millions. **Forward mode** carries a derivative along with each value. Choose an input direction (for the partial derivative with respect to x₁, seed ẋ₁ = 1 and ẋ₂ = 0) and propagate the **tangent** v̇_i = ∂v_i/∂(seed) forward, applying the local derivative rule at each step.

example.title: Forward mode for ∂f/∂x₁
example.problem: Propagate tangents through the trace of the previous example with the seed ẋ₁ = 1, ẋ₂ = 0 at (2, 5).
solution: v̇₃ = v̇₁/v₁ = 0.5. v̇₄ = v̇₁v₂ + v₁v̇₂ = 5 + 0 = 5. v̇₅ = cos(v₂)·v̇₂ = 0.
So ∂f/∂x₁ = 5.5, matching the hand calculation. To get ∂f/∂x₂ we run again with the seed (0, 1): 1.7163.

body: Forward mode computes a **Jacobian–vector product** J·v: the derivative of all outputs in one chosen input direction, at about the cost of one evaluation of the program (two to three times, for the extra multiplications). A full Jacobian with n inputs takes n passes.

A **dual number** a + bε with ε² = 0 stores a value and its derivative. Arithmetic on dual numbers carries out the forward-mode rules automatically: (a + bε)(c + dε) = ac + (ad + bc)ε, the product rule.

code: other = other if isinstance(other, Dual) else Dual(other)

def sin(x): return Dual(math.sin(x.value), math.cos(x.value) * x.tangent)
def log(x): return Dual(math.log(x.value), x.tangent / x.value)
out = f(Dual(2.0, 1.0), Dual(5.0, 0.0))      # seed the tangent of x1
body.caption: Forward mode in 20 lines: the program f is unchanged, only the numbers are replaced by dual numbers.

body: Forward mode is efficient when there are few inputs and many outputs, and for directional derivatives and Jacobian–vector products. It needs no memory beyond the current values.

check.q: Forward mode with one seed vector computes
check.a: a Jacobian–vector product, the derivative of all outputs along one input direction
wrong: the full gradient of a scalar loss

sections.title: Reverse mode: backpropagation
body: Reverse mode asks the opposite question: for the final output, how much does each earlier quantity matter? Imagine finding out who is responsible for a mistake by tracing back from the result, one step at a time. A single backward pass gives the effect of every input on the one output, which is exactly the situation for a loss with millions of parameters. **Reverse mode** goes the other way. It first runs the program forward, recording the trace. Then it propagates **adjoints** v̄_i = ∂f/∂v_i, the sensitivity of the final output to each intermediate variable, from the output backward. At each step, the adjoint of a variable is the sum over the operations that used it of (adjoint of the result) × (local derivative).

example.title: Reverse mode for the whole gradient
example.problem: Compute both partial derivatives of the previous function at (2, 5) in one backward pass.
solution: Start with v̄₇ = 1. The step v₇ = v₆ − v₅ gives v̄₆ = v̄₇ = 1 and v̄₅ = −v̄₇ = −1.
v₅ = sin v₂: v̄₂ gets −cos(5) = −0.2837 from this step.
v₄ = v₁v₂: v̄₁ gets v̄₄·v₂ = 5 and v̄₂ gets v̄₄·v₁ = 2.
v₃ = ln v₁: v̄₁ gets v̄₃/v₁ = 0.5.
Totals: v̄₁ = 5 + 0.5 = 5.5 and v̄₂ = −0.2837 + 2 = 1.7163. One backward pass gave both partial derivatives.

body: Reverse mode computes a **vector–Jacobian product** vᵀJ. For a function with a single scalar output (a loss) this is the entire gradient. The **cheap gradient principle**: the gradient of a scalar function costs only a small constant multiple (typically 2 to 4 times) of evaluating the function, regardless of the number of inputs. For a network with a million weights, that is a million times cheaper than finite differences, and the reason deep learning is feasible.

table.caption: Forward versus reverse mode.

body: The backward pass needs the intermediate values of the forward pass (the local derivatives depend on them), so reverse mode stores them: memory proportional to the number of operations, typically the activations of a network times the batch size. Remedies are **gradient checkpointing** (store only some intermediate values and recompute the rest in the backward pass: with L layers, storing about √L checkpoints gives O(√L) memory at the price of one extra forward pass), lower precision, and smaller batches (see Computer Systems).

list: **Higher derivatives**: a Hessian–vector product Hv can be computed at the cost of a few gradients by differentiating the gradient (forward mode over reverse mode), without forming the n × n Hessian. It is used for Newton–CG methods, for curvature estimates and for the second-order terms of some meta-learning methods.
**Jacobians**: the full Jacobian of a map ℝⁿ → ℝᵐ needs min(n, m) passes. For m = 1 the gradient needs one.

check.a: one backward pass gives the gradient of a scalar loss with respect to all parameters

it works only for linear networks

check.q: The main cost of reverse mode is
check.a: memory for the intermediate values of the forward pass
wrong: many extra forward passes, one per parameter

sections.title: A small reverse-mode engine
body: A reverse-mode engine needs three things: a node that stores a value, its gradient, the nodes it was computed from and a rule to send gradients back to them; a topological ordering of the graph; and a backward pass in reverse topological order that **accumulates** (adds) gradients, since a node used twice receives a contribution from each use.

for v in reversed(order):                # outputs first, inputs last
body.caption: A reverse-mode autodiff engine in the style of Karpathy's micrograd. The gradients are ∂c/∂a = b = −3 and ∂c/∂b = a + 2b = −4.

list: Gradients are **accumulated with +=**, because a variable can feed several operations (here b is used in a * b and in b ** 2: its gradient is the sum of both contributions: a from the product plus 2b from the square, 2 − 6 = −4).
The topological ordering (from Graph Algorithms) guarantees that a node's gradient is complete before it is sent on to its parents.
Adding an operation to the engine requires only its forward computation and the rule that maps the output gradient to the input gradients, i.e. the vector–Jacobian product of that operation.
Real frameworks work on whole tensors, not scalars: the rule for a matrix product C = AB sends Ā = C̄Bᵀ and B̄ = AᵀC̄, the equations of backpropagation.

check.q: Why must gradients be accumulated (added) in the backward pass?
check.a: A variable used by several operations receives a gradient contribution from each use
wrong: To average the gradient over the batch

sections.title: Autodiff in practice: PyTorch and JAX
body: Deep learning frameworks provide AD as a core feature.

code: x = torch.tensor(2.0, requires_grad=True)    # track operations on x
y = x ** 2 + 3 * x                           # builds the graph as it runs
loss.backward()                              # w.grad is the gradient of the loss
with torch.no_grad():                        # update without recording the operation
w.grad.zero_()                               # gradients accumulate: reset before the next step
body.caption: PyTorch: the graph is recorded as the code runs (dynamic graph), so ordinary Python control flow works.

code: grad_loss = jax.grad(loss)                   # a function that returns the gradient w.r.t. w
fast_grad = jax.jit(grad_loss)               # compile it for speed
per_example = jax.vmap(grad_loss, in_axes=(None, 0, 0))   # one gradient per example
body.caption: JAX treats differentiation as a function transformation: grad, jit and vmap compose.

list: **PyTorch** records a **dynamic graph** during the forward pass: easy to debug, flexible control flow. **TensorFlow 1** built a static graph first; **JAX** traces functions into a graph and compiles them with XLA; both give the compiler a global view for fusion and optimization (see Roofline).

**Gradient accumulation**: PyTorch adds new gradients into .grad on every backward call. Reset them with zero_grad() each step, or exploit the behavior to simulate a large batch by accumulating the gradients of several small ones before one update.
**Detaching** a tensor (.detach(), torch.no_grad()) cuts it out of the graph. Use it for evaluation, for target values in reinforcement learning, and for the frozen parts of a network.

**Non-differentiable operations** (argmax, rounding, sampling, comparison) have zero or undefined derivative. Remedies are smooth surrogates (softmax for argmax), the straight-through estimator (pass the gradient as if the operation were the identity), and the reparameterization trick for sampling (see VAEs).
**In-place operations** (x += 1) can overwrite a value that the backward pass needs, and the framework raises an error. Prefer out-of-place operations on tensors that take part in the graph.

**Custom gradients**: for an operation that is numerically unstable or has a known better derivative (a stable log-sum-exp, an implicit layer, a fused kernel), the user supplies the backward rule explicitly.
**Checking**: compare against finite differences on small inputs (gradient checking), as in Software Practice.

body.tip: When a gradient is None, zero or nan, trace backward: was the tensor created with requires_grad, did an operation detach it, did a non-differentiable operation intervene, or did the forward pass already contain a nan? Printing the gradient of intermediate tensors (retain_grad) locates the break.

check.a: add the new gradients to the existing ones
wrong: raise an error in all cases

check.a: passing gradients through a non-differentiable operation such as rounding

summary: Automatic differentiation applies the chain rule to the elementary operations that a program executes. It is exact up to rounding, unlike finite differences, and never builds a symbolic formula.

Forward mode propagates tangents alongside values (dual numbers) and gives a Jacobian–vector product per pass; reverse mode runs the program, records the trace, and propagates adjoints backward, giving a vector–Jacobian product per pass.

For a scalar loss with n parameters, reverse mode computes the whole gradient at a small constant multiple of the forward cost; its price is the memory of the stored intermediate values, reduced by checkpointing.
A reverse-mode engine needs nodes with local backward rules, a topological order and accumulation of gradients; the framework operates on tensors with the matrix rules of backpropagation.

PyTorch records a dynamic graph and accumulates .grad; JAX transforms functions with grad, jit and vmap. Watch for detaching, in-place operations, non-differentiable operations and the need to reset gradients.

problems.q: For f(x, y) = x·y + sin(x), compute f and ∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y at (1, 2) by forward mode (two passes) and by reverse mode (one pass).
problems.solution: Trace: v₁ = x = 1, v₂ = y = 2, v₃ = v₁v₂ = 2, v₄ = sin v₁ = 0.8415, v₅ = v₃ + v₄ = 2.8415. Forward, seed (1, 0): v̇₃ = 2, v̇₄ = cos 1 = 0.5403, v̇₅ = 2.5403. Seed (0, 1): v̇₃ = 1, v̇₄ = 0, v̇₅ = 1. Reverse: v̄₅ = 1, v̄₃ = v̄₄ = 1; v̄₁ = v̄₃ v₂ + v̄₄ cos v₁ = 2 + 0.5403 = 2.5403; v̄₂ = v̄₃ v₁ = 1.

problems.q: Run the micro engine of the text by hand for c = a * b with a = 3, b = 4, then for c = a * a.
problems.solution: For c = a*b: a.grad = b = 4 and b.grad = a = 3. For c = a*a, the same node is used twice. The backward rule adds both contributions: a.grad = a + a = 6 = 2a, which is the derivative of a². This is why gradients must be accumulated.

problems.q: A function maps ℝ¹⁰⁰⁰ → ℝ³. How many forward-mode and reverse-mode passes are needed for its full Jacobian? Which would you use?
problems.solution: Forward mode needs one pass per input: 1000. Reverse mode needs one per output: 3. Use reverse mode.
problems.a: 1000 forward passes versus 3 reverse passes; reverse mode.

problems.q: A network has 64 layers, and each layer's activations occupy 200 MB for a batch. How much memory do the stored activations need, and how much if every 8th layer is checkpointed and the rest are recomputed in segments of 8 (assume at most one segment is held at a time)?
problems.solution: Without checkpointing: 64 × 200 MB = 12.8 GB. With checkpointing every 8th layer: 8 checkpoints (1.6 GB) plus one segment of 8 layers being recomputed (1.6 GB): about 3.2 GB, roughly a quarter, at the cost of one extra forward pass (about 33% more compute).

problems.q: Using the dual-number approach, find the derivative of g(x) = x³ + 2x at x = 2 by hand with the tangent seeded to 1.
